title: Stones and candles
hook: a stone left on a grave, and a candle each year on the yahrzeit

segments.voice: Yesterday, shloshim: thirty days, and for a parent, much of the year. Your line was slowly back. How did you mark your month? Today, the last lesson on the life cycle, and what stays after the year is over. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-five.

A Jewish cemetery on a weekday afternoon. No funeral. Just rows of headstones, and on top of some of them, small stones. A gray pebble. A chip of granite. A smooth one from a beach somewhere, carried a long way in a pocket. Nobody sells them at the gate. People bring them, or bend down and pick one up from the path. Some graves have one. Some have a little crowd. And somewhere across town, on a kitchen counter, a candle in a glass is burning in the middle of an ordinary day, and nobody blows it out. Two small objects. Today they finish the life cycle.
screen: `SMALL STONES ON A HEADSTONE.` → `NOBODY SELLS THEM.` → `A CANDLE ON THE COUNTER.`

segments.voice: Stones and candles. Turn it four ways. First, the stone. There's no single agreed reason for the custom. People give several. Flowers wilt, and a stone doesn't. A stone tells the family someone came, even if nobody saw them. And there's an old picture behind it: in Genesis, when Rachel dies on the road, "Jacob set up a pillar upon her grave." A stone that says, she was here, and she was loved. Second, the candle. Each year, on the anniversary of a death by the Hebrew calendar, families mark the yahrzeit, a Yiddish word for that day. A candle is lit at home and left to burn through the day. People often connect it to a line from Proverbs: "The spirit of man is the lamp of the LORD." A small flame for a whole life. Third, what goes with it. On the yahrzeit, children say Kaddish for a parent, and some give to charity or study a little Torah in their memory. The dead are remembered by the living doing good. Fourth, the whole block. This block began with the idea that a life has rituals. Then a baby welcomed at the door, a covenant, a daughter's name, a first haircut, honey on the letters. Coming of age. A match, a canopy, seven blessings, a broken glass, peace in the home. Then the holy society, plain wood, the tear, the shovel, seven days, thirty days. And now a pebble and a flame. From the first welcome to the last stone, nobody passes through a Jewish life alone.
screen: `WHY A STONE? SEVERAL ANSWERS.` · `A CANDLE FOR THE YAHRZEIT.` · `REMEMBERED BY DOING GOOD.` · `THE LIFE CYCLE, LOOKED BACK ON.` · then, large: `STONES REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a small stone. Settle, and breathe. If there's a stone or pebble near you, hold it. If not, picture one. Feel its weight, its edges, how cool it is. Bring to mind someone who has died, someone you knew, or someone you've only heard about. Let the stone stand for one thing you remember about them. When you can, leave it somewhere that means something: on a grave, at a window, on a shelf, by a door. If you pray, you can remember them in your prayer. The bell holds the time.
Stones and candles. A pebble left on a grave to say someone came, and a flame each year on the yahrzeit. Today's word.
Your line: stones remember. Today, leave your small stone somewhere meaningful, and say the person's name once as you set it down. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-five.

howItsDone: Jewish visitors to a grave often leave a small stone on the headstone, and each year on the yahrzeit, the anniversary of a death, families light a memorial candle at home, and children say Kaddish for a parent.
